metadata.title: House rejects bid to curb Trump's war powers on Iran

left: The U.S. House of Representatives voted 219 to 212 to reject a resolution that would have halted President Trump's military actions against Iran and required congressional authorization for further attacks.

The War Powers Resolution of 1973 requires that unauthorized military actions must end within 60 days unless Congress authorizes their continuation; the Trump administration cites an imminent threat from Iran to justify current actions.

Supporters and opponents of the resolution differed on constitutional grounds, with supporters advocating for Congress's role in authorizing war and opponents arguing for the legality of presidential action to defend the U.S. against threats.
The vote largely followed party lines, with Republicans backing the president's actions and Democrats criticizing the lack of clear objectives and congressional approval.
center: On Thursday, the Republican-controlled House of Representatives voted down a bipartisan resolution directing President Donald Trump to end U.S. military operations in Iran, with the measure failing 219 to 212 one day after the Senate blocked a similar resolution.

Citing the Constitution and the 1973 War Powers Resolution, supporters argued Congress should reassert its authority, as Rep. Thomas Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna authored the bipartisan measure after Trump submitted the resolution on Tuesday.
Casualty figures underscore the stakes, as six Americans have been killed in the conflict so far, and observers say failed votes grant implicit authorization for U.S. strikes that began last weekend.
The House vote was widely described as symbolic, and Rep. Thomas Massie acknowledged the measure was headed for defeat, while some Republicans said the issue could return if the war expands.
Despite campaign rhetoric against new wars, critics said the resolution's failure reflected Republican deference to Trump, with House leadership pushing back earlier this week.
right: The U.S. House of Representatives narrowly rejected a bipartisan war powers resolution to halt President Donald Trump's military actions against Iran by a 212-219 vote, following a similar Senate defeat along party lines.

Republicans mostly support Trump's actions against Iran, viewing them as a necessary response to threats, while Democrats, joined by a few Republicans, oppose the conflict and argue that Congress should authorize any military actions.

An alternative resolution allowing 30 days for congressional approval of military actions was introduced following the vote; there is ongoing debate over war powers and defense funding related to the conflict.
